scope: Amodo's own status report of a built tray-level retrofit sensor suite (cameras with OpenCV intrusion detection, PIR, temperature, pressure, IMU, tamper mesh, lid switch, time-of-flight; STM32 TrustZone controller; power-down response) in an RFD still marked 'idea'; no detection or false-alarm rate, no skilled-attacker test (red-team and stress testing are listed as future work), no dataset. The seals clause has no held test: the 289-seal assessment that found all could be defeated cheaply is named by Aarne, Fist & Withers (2024) but not held, so it is not Failed here; 'TamperSec working on this (?)' in the Proofworks projects list is hearsay; Harack et al.'s glitter-and-photograph suggestion is untested. The headline's 'under skilled covert attack' clause has no work.
doc: AI Security Forum (2025), Requests for Discussion, RFD 028 Retrofittable Tamper Detection System (Amodo)
quote: Amodo's v0.1 system includes 8 countermeasures selected from 38 candidates after reviewing 27 attack vectors. … Cameras (4 per tray, OpenCV-based intrusion detection) … Successfully demonstrated detection using STM built-in logic

scope: Design options only, for enclosures around accelerators dissipating up to 1,200 W: active sensing by capacitance, resistance mesh, radio response or distributed sensors; response by key deletion or permanent disablement (capacitor discharge, antifuses, nanothermite); cooling pass-through by a thin boundary under the cold plate, a contained liquid loop with a boundary heat exchanger, or metalised foam for air; enclosure sizes from chip to rack. Nothing built at this scale, no red team, no false-trigger rate; the authors judge that nation-state attackers can likely compromise the best current enclosures and that the per-device cost of circumvention is hard to estimate. The sensing prototypes the section cites are not held. Cross-references, not evidence for this headline: Immler et al. (2019) built and attacked a PCB-scale PUF cover (enclosure PUFs problem); Amodo's tray-level sensor retrofit with power-down response (seals and sensor suites problem) is not an enclosure.
doc: Petrie & Aarne (2025), Technical Options for Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 2)
quote: Secure enclosures can ideally be made compatible with both air and direct to chip liquid cooling … To permit cooling, the secure enclosure boundary can either be sandwiched between the chip face and cooling pad, or it can contain both the chip and the cooling pad. If it is sandwiched beneath the cooling pad, it has to be very thin and very thermally conductive.

scope: Batteryless flexPCB mesh cover deriving a PUF key for a multi-chip PCB embedded system, aiming at FIPS 140-2 Level 3: statistics over 115 covers, physical attacks, and a -20 to +60 C chamber test on one board with three covers plus accelerated ageing of foils. Not accelerator scale or 700–1,200 W, no vibration test, and multi-year key stability not shown (the authors suggest re-enrolling in the field), so the headline's years-of-cycling clause is open; probing resistance is argued by design (keys not reachable without destroying the PUF) rather than tested against microprobing. Kulp et al. (2024) report the demonstration second-hand; the stability question is posed as open by Harack et al. (2025) and the RAND PUF-enclosures RFD.
doc: Immler, Obermaier, Ng, Ke, Lee, Lim, Oh, Wee & Sigl (2019), Secure Physical Enclosures from Covers with Tamper-Resistance (IACR TCHES)
quote: We demonstrate the feasibility of our concept … Practical results including statistics over a set of 115 flexPCB covers, physical attacks, and environmental testing support our design rationale.

scope: Non-destructive, measured on hardware: an on-FPGA network analyser reads the board's power-delivery-network impedance and flags an added shunt resistor, removed decoupling capacitors, a nearby EM probe and a polished package on commercial FPGA development boards, one board per tamper event, with a global threshold that gave no false alarms on the authors' own measurements. Not a detection and false-alarm rate across devices; not a data-centre GPU board; circuit edits inside the package (FIB) and re-encapsulation are not covered. Related held work: BackMon (Mosavirik & Tajik 2024) detects removal of the cooling stack exposing a flip-chip die backside, one board, no error rates; Safa et al. 2023 use VNA impedance signatures to spot aged chips. The headline is not answered within a stated scope.
doc: Mosavirik, Schaumont & Tajik (2022), ImpedanceVerif: On-Chip Impedance Sensing for System-Level Tampering Detection (IACR TCHES 2023, no. 1)
quote: The magnitude of the WD metric shows that all tamper events performed in this paper can be distinguished if we use the sensor at the right frequency. Moreover, the detection thresholds for different tamper events, and their corresponding frequency bands, can be selected differently. However, we still can define a global threshold at W D = 3 for the tampering experiments presented in this work without causing any false alarms.

scope: Desk study only: a literature survey of physical side channels and an example defence architecture for rack or pod enclosures, with an estimated bill of materials below 1% of cluster cost while tolerating single-digit kbit/s of covert bandwidth; the author calls it a two-week sprint, 'far from conclusive'. Nothing built; no facility or pod red-teamed; no verified leakage limit; the RF attenuation of cheaply welded sheet-metal enclosures is an assumption, not a measurement. Single-computer exfiltration demonstrations held in the collection (Fansmitter acoustic exfiltration at 15 bits/min, Deep-TEMPEST HDMI, Synesthesia screen acoustics) are attack measurements at PC scale, not containment tests, and are cross-references because the headline names facility or pod scale. The Proofworks workshop 'seeming consensus' that 1-bit air-gapping is feasible is an opinion.
doc: Cankaya (2026), Suppressing Side Channels in an Untrusted Data Center via Retrofitted Defenses (MIRI TGT blog)
quote: I present an example of a defense architecture towards the end of this post. It leverages a synergy of cheap enclosures, sensors, jamming, unannounced hardware inspections and physical security

scope: Measured failure rates on real field data: 18,688 NVIDIA K20X GPUs on ORNL's Titan (2012–2019), survival analysis, with about 11,000 boards replaced for a resistor-corrosion defect; corroborated by Bode et al. 2021 on Blue Waters (4,228 K20X GPUs, roughly 0.0035 replacements per GPU-year, no wear-out rise). Limits: decade-old GPUs in maintained, air-cooled HPC machines, not a sealed cluster of current accelerators. The spare and redundancy fraction clause has no work: Dean's 2025 hazard-rate note (0.001–0.18 per year) is a desk estimate drawn from these datasets and gives no spares fraction; the flexHEG, Harack and AISF rows are open questions.
doc: Ostrouchov et al. (2020), GPU Lifetimes on Titan Supercomputer: Survival Analysis and Reliability (ORNL)
quote: We write about the last rework cycle and a reliability analysis of over 100,000 years of GPU lifetimes during Titan’s 6-year-long productive period. Using time between failures analysis and statistical survival analysis techniques, we find that GPU reliability is dependent on heat dissipation to an extent that strongly correlates with detailed nuances of the cooling architecture and job scheduling.

scope: A desk estimate conditional on the AI 2040 Plan A regime, in which chip production is monitored at a small number of controlled fabs and upstream suppliers' purchases, inventory and cumulative production are declared and cross-checked layer by layer; concealed domestic production is given a 25% feasibility that the authors call an intuitive guess. Shavit (2023) proposes production-line monitoring on the nuclear-fuel model and tracking the lithography supply chain to detect new fabs, without a precision. No fab's output has been bounded by measurement and no covert-fab detection method has been tested.
doc: Halstead & Larsen (2026), Covert AI Projects (AI 2040 Plan A supplement)
quote: Concretely, we should be able to keep diversion to approximately zero and have very high confidence that total diversion is less than 100k H100e.

scope: A proposed custody principle only: verifiable transport at each step from fab through dicing and packaging, with liability on the last holder; no mechanism, miss rate or test. Cankaya (2025) describes signed ECID handoffs second-hand from Zhang & Guin (2019), which is not held, and leaves 'who last had custody' for a later post; Scher & Thiergart list CISA-style chain-of-custody documentation as a building block. Nothing deployed for an AI-accelerator supply chain.
doc: Shavit (2023), What Does It Take to Catch a Chinchilla? Verifying Rules on Large-Scale Neural Network Training via Compute Monitoring
quote: it is important for the wafers (and later the dies) to be securely and verifiably transported at each step. If these chip precursors ever go missing, responsibility for the violation would lie with the most recent holder.

scope: A design for an international body's oversight of guarantee-processor production: manufacturing equipment locked to the approved design, independent testing by a party other than the manufacturer, continuous camera and on-site staff oversight, tamper-evident shipping, extensive testing and imaging of a 1/1000 sample (the authors' own arithmetic gives a 63% chance of catching a 1,000-device compromised batch), verifiable destruction of failed devices, published processes and authorised penetration tests. Nothing instituted or piloted. Oversight of accelerator fabs themselves is only an analogy to nuclear-fuel monitoring (Shavit 2023); retroactive trust in already-produced chips is a proposal to sample and destructively reverse-engineer existing components (flexHEG Part 1). No held document reports any oversight regime in operation.
doc: Aarne & Petrie (2025), International Security Applications of Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 3)
quote: Each guarantee processor should be subjected to automated, independent testing. … the testing should be done by a different party than the one that manufactured it, ideally either by the international body, several member states, or both.

scope: Software (atomic-race) fingerprint telling apart 24 same-model H200 GPUs rented on vast.ai, 480 runs; up to 100% paired re-identification. The authors' own limitations: not validated at larger scale; stability over time, transport and temperature not established; security against an adversary who emulates the GPU or runs the function faster not tested, so the headline's 'cannot defeat by swapping in another chip' clause and a published false-match rate at scale remain open. Lower-ranked evidence: Alpay & Alpay (2026) measure a per-SM latency map stable over a six-hour RTX 5090 run and 100% leave-one-out separation across distinct Blackwell dies, but leave same-model die separation to prior work; Safa, Mosavirik & Tajik (2023) distinguish an aged STM32 from 10–12 genuine ones by S-parameters with no error rates. No cost figure in any held source.
doc: Tee & Happel (2026), GPU Fingerprinting for Location Verification (TAIGR @ ICML 2026, arXiv 2605.01930v2)
quote: we evaluated the function across 24 Nvidia H200 GPUs, 2 seeds, and 10 runs each … fingerprinting function that achieved up to 100% accuracy in small-scale tests

scope: A proposal only: the non-manufacturing side samples fabricated components and destructively reverse-engineers them against the manufacturer's design documents; flexHEG Part 2 adds open-sourcing the guarantee-processor design for comparison with physical scans of randomly selected chips, and Ilhan et al. (2026) analyse physical inspection and sampling as the direct check. No held document reports a third party checking a fabricated die against its design, and none gives a detection rate on a deliberately inserted mismatch; the only rate is Agrawal et al. (2007), a circuit-level power simulation (49/49 simulated Trojan chips caught, 1/49 false alarm) on a 28k-gate RSA core, no silicon measured. Puschner et al.'s real-world SEM Trojan-detection case study is named by the Proofworks neutral-compute note but not held.
doc: Petrie, Aarne, Ammann & Dalrymple (2025), Overview of Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 1)
quote: some of the existing components could be sampled for rigorous, destructive reverse-engineering to check that they match the design documents provided by the manufacturer.

scope: A desk analysis of the sampling clause: inspection cost and sample size against Trojan prevalence, with the observation that sampling 1% of chips may cost more than producing all chips unverified; Aarne & Petrie (2025, flexHEG Part 3) give the same arithmetic for a 1/1000 sampling rate (63% chance of catching a 1,000-device compromised batch). No held document measures per-die cost, time or miss rate of destructive or non-destructive inspection at an advanced node: Harack et al. (2025) state no non-destructive technique is known for a chip with tens of billions of transistors, and Ilhan et al. call inspection 'extremely expensive, slow, and often destructive' without numbers. Cross-references, not evidence for this headline: Agrawal et al. (2007) simulate side-channel screening (no silicon); Thummala et al. (2026) measure a power side-channel screen on one Atmel microcontroller (93.2% of tampered-firmware traces flagged at 1% false positives), firmware tampering rather than die modification.
doc: Ilhan, Withers, Gietz & Harack (2026), Verifiable Semiconductor Manufacturing (Oxford AIGI)
quote: If only 1 chip in 100,000 is compromised, many thousands must be tested to achieve high confidence of detection. The sampling regime can be tuned based on acceptable risk (e.g., testing 1% of chips vs 0.01%), but this involves significant cost considerations.

scope: Design options only, for the guarantee processor: open-sourcing the design and logic for third-party analysis against physical scans of randomly selected chips, executing guarantee logic on publicly auditable FPGAs, and running redundant guarantee processors from different manufacturers in lock-step; flexHEG Part 3 adds collaborative design with justification of every choice. Nothing built, no outside review of real silicon, and no detection rate on seeded trojans anywhere in the held sources; the binning clause (dormant functionality) has only RAND's design rule that there be none.
doc: Petrie & Aarne (2025), Technical Options for Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 2)
quote: To increase trust that backdoors have not been added to the Guarantee Processor design or manufacturing process, some options are: … Open-sourcing the guarantee processor design and guarantee logic, which could then be analyzed and compared with physical scans of randomly selected chips.

scope: A desk analysis of the fab-process clause: repurposing fabs' existing process-data anomaly detection and virtual metrology for security, with its stated limits (catches only attacks that show as statistical deviations; high false-positive risk in a noisy fab). No detection rate anywhere. The design-flow clause rests on graph-neural-network detectors trained on netlists reported second-hand (Thorat et al. 2025, not held), which flag patterns resembling known Trojans rather than unseen families; no held document tests any detector at accelerator scale or on unseen trojan families. Logic locking and other obfuscation are described in the same paper as broken by SAT-style attacks, but those attack papers are not held.
doc: Ilhan, Withers, Gietz & Harack (2026), Verifiable Semiconductor Manufacturing (Oxford AIGI)
quote: A more scalable approach is to integrate verification into the fabrication process itself. Modern fabs already collect enormous amounts of process data for yield and quality control, including sensor readings, optical inspections of masks and wafers, and electrical test parameters. By applying statistical anomaly detection to this data, one can attempt to catch deviations that might indicate tampering.

scope: A design answer to the neutral-producer clause: redundant guarantee processors from each bloc and nested enclosures each built by a different bloc, with the integration details left out of scope; the Proofworks neutral-compute note sketches the alternative of open-sourcing designs down to GDSII and fabricating on trailing nodes, which it judges impossible at the leading edge. The end-to-end chain clause has Ilhan et al.'s (2026) analysis of layered design-phase and manufacturing-phase measures, with the chain itself posed as an open question. Nothing built; no neutral producer identified (the Proofworks prospects note sees no candidate in a US–China scenario). One colour: both clauses are answered by the same hardware supply-chain security community, so the sorting-pass split is not used.
doc: Aarne & Petrie (2025), International Security Applications of Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 3)
quote: they might instead rely on a design where different countries provide different overlapping components of the design, such that each country can trust the system without trusting all of the components. … security processors could be redundant, such that everything passes through two chips that implement the same specifications, one designed and manufactured by each bloc.

scope: A desk analysis drawing on industry conversations: which governance mechanisms the installed base could take by firmware alone (the H100's security module, TEE and secure boot are noted as present), with timeline estimates by threat context (months for firmware-only, 18 months to 4 years for silicon changes, several years for tamper-proofing) and the caveat that existing secure-boot implementations likely carry unpatchable flaws. External-module retrofit is a design option in flexHEG Part 2 (capacitor-based disablement 'a good option for retrofitting'; antifuses unsuitable). No held document demonstrates a retrofit or states what fraction of installed compute cannot take one; Shavit (2023) notes many sold chips may be neither retrofittable nor locatable. Brass & Aarne (2024), cited by Tee & Happel for delay-based location verification on existing confidential-computing keys, is not held.
doc: Aarne, Fist & Withers (2024), Secure, Governable Chips (CNAS)
quote: For minimally adversarial contexts the current level of hardware security likely would be sufficient, and thus many mechanisms could be implemented as firmware updates. This would take a few months. Some mechanisms may not be possible to implement this way on current hardware, in which case silicon-level changes would be required, and the time to implement them would increase to between 18 months and 4 years.

scope: A requirements design for the read path (attested enclave or secure-boot-chained firmware, hardware-rooted signing, nonce-binding against replay, attested monitoring software), pointing to the flexHEG guarantee-processor designs; nothing built, and no shipping GPU is named as having it - every source says such paths 'do not yet exist'. Telemetry accuracy (sampling fraction, counter error) is in the statement but not the headline: related, with measured work (Yang et al. 2023: only 25% of runtime sampled for power on A100/H100).
doc: Rahman & Tajdari (2026), Detecting Hidden ML Training With Zero-Overhead Telemetry (MIRI; arXiv 2606.19262)
quote: The monitoring agent must read counter values from a source the adversary cannot tamper with—e.g., an attested enclave on the GPU firmware boundary (Aarne et al., 2025) or a verified read path through secure-boot-chained firmware (Petrie, 2025; O’Gara et al., 2025). Without this, an adversary with software privilege simply returns forged values.

scope: One NVIDIA A100 model, one driver, one cluster; energy read from on-die telemetry with a perfect meter assumed; the authors' own adversary model; the bound tightens to about 0.06 only with re-execution at an observed operating point; a 0.41-1.16 gap left open. The loosening from on-die to feed meter and the multi-device facility bound are explicitly not addressed ('assume a perfect meter'; 'do not offer a facility-level, multi-device version'), so that clause has no work.
doc: Kimpson, Baker & Graham (2026), Can Power Draw Constrain Covert Compute? Limits of Analogue Verification for AI Governance (arXiv 2610.07476v1)
quote: Measurements on NVIDIA A100 GPUs constrain β = 1.16 in the worst case, while adversarial matched-energy strategies are shown to hide at least β = 0.41 of compute.

scope: A paper design from a research sprint the author calls 'a first-pass viability study': enclosures, sensors, look-through jamming, inspections and physical security with an estimated bill of materials below 1% of cluster cost (this survey's cost goal of 1% of facility cost, met on paper only); power-filter volume cost 'has proven difficult' to pin down; no attenuation or leakage-rate cap measured; the 39 dB look-through suppression is cited from commodity radios in work not held; wardens: no work ('unexplored').
doc: Cankaya (2026), Suppressing Side Channels in an Untrusted Data Center via Retrofitted Defenses (MIRI TGT blog)
quote: I present an example of a defense architecture towards the end of this post. It leverages a synergy of cheap enclosures, sensors, jamming, unannounced hardware inspections and physical security … at an estimated (!) Bill-of-Materials (BOM) below 1% of the cost of the monitored cluster

scope: Leakage of verifier-facing releases derived from real physical measurements (H100 and B200 node power traces, RAPL power traces, GPU electromagnetic traces, measured workload profiles) over six verification tasks, measured as conditional mutual information: this covers the prover's quantified leak bound for what the verifier receives. The verifier-trusts-the-readings clause is out of scope ('MID does not make a compromised evidence source honest'); exfiltration by the sensor hardware itself (bits per second per channel) and a mutually trusted sensor: nothing built; Harack's prover-side mitigations are paper only.
doc: Abdelghafar & Kulp (2026), Privacy-Preserving AI Verification via Minimal Information Disclosure (arXiv 2608.02774v1)
quote: Across these tasks, MID produces three releases with perfect held-out verification and zero measured collateral leakage, while the remaining tasks yield explicit privacy–utility frontiers.

scope: One normalized production training trace on DGX-H100 racks (no GPU count, model or absolute power): a 0.2-3 Hz band and an iteration dip recurring 'from once per second or less, to once every tens of seconds'. Dip duty cycle, step-time jitter and harmonic amplitudes at chip, rack and facility meter are not reported. Node level: Vercellino et al. (2026), also held, measure 4xH100 node power at 0.1 s for fine-tuning and training up to 16 nodes. Facility meter: simulation only (Ko & Zhu 2026, whose assumed 0.5-1.5 Hz iteration rate conflicts with Choukse; Vercellino's stitched facility profiles) and an unattributed once-a-second grid sag at a data-center substation (Mishra et al. 2025).
doc: Choukse et al. (2025), Power Stabilization for AI Training Datacenters (Microsoft, OpenAI, NVIDIA; arXiv 2508.14318v2)
quote: AI workload power traces like those in Figure 1 show FFT energy concentrated between 0.2–3 Hz (Figure 3)—close to known resonant modes of turbine-generator shafts and long transmission lines.

scope: Steganography in inference outputs only: the authors' own detector on open-weight models of 3B-30B parameters under their trust assumptions (every input, output and seed logged; honest verification server). Protocol free variables: Cankaya's Fermi estimate of about 100 bits per second through active north-south taps, which he calls informed guesses needing validation - paper only. Physical channels (fibre, coolant, RF): Cankaya's side-channel survey estimates ('we expect Mbps to be possible'; 'strong case studies are few') - paper only; NVLink contention: no work. Older covert-channel measurements in the collection (Ethernet padding, thermal) were not made against compute monitoring.
doc: Rinberg, Karvonen, Hoover, Reuter & Warr (2025), Verifying LLM Inference to Detect Model Weight Exfiltration (arXiv 2511.02620v3)
quote: On MOE-Qwen-30B, our detector reduces exfiltratable information to < 0.5% with false-positive rate of < 10−2 , corresponding to a > 200× slowdown for adversaries.

scope: Design only: a neutrally located, mutually monitored and possibly air-gapped data centre runs privacy-preserving evaluations, assessors emit one bit per judgment, and the sensitive data is verifiably deleted afterwards (Fig. 2.1 caption); how the bit is transferred is left to future work (fn 261). The fault-and-retry leakage budget appears only as a stated requirement in Cankaya's self-deprecated System Overview v0.2 (a pre-agreed budgeted fault rate). Nothing built, no red-team, no measured leak bound.
doc: Harack et al. (2025), Verification for International AI Governance (Oxford AIGI)
quote: After conducting their evaluations as agreed by the Prover and Verifier, the assessor would be able to reliably transmit one bit per judgment to the Verifier and Prover.

scope: Hashing every frame on one 400GbE link with generator traffic on real hardware: line rate holds for frames of 1500 B and above on a 32-core CPU, fails for 64 B frames and on DPU offload - a prover choosing small frames defeats complete hashing. This is the capture layer only; reconciling hashed egress against an inference log to a stated confidence, red-team exfiltration tests, and the inference-site architecture (weights path over partitioned networks and data diodes, where 'we have not seen any work') are paper only or no work. The designs are Cankaya's north-south taps with all egress 'fully explainable' by observed activity and Rinberg's Merkle inference ledger. The same benchmark is the evidence for the traffic-hashing problem.
doc: Reynolds & Foster (2026), Network Traffic Hashing (Amodo Design note)
quote: For worst-case 64B minimum frames, no algorithm on this hardware reaches full line rate … For realistic traffic profiles at 1500B and above, AES-128-GMAC and SipHash-1-3-128 are both capable of sustaining line-rate hashing

scope: The authors' own measurement of their own method on rented cloud GPUs with cooperative hosts: network-delay geolocation against public RIPE Atlas landmarks places a B200 within 44 km and a V100 within 270 km (79-298 km depending on landmark density) and rejects 11 of 11 decoy sites; the decoys are other locations, not an adversary adding delay or relaying, and the paper says a high round-trip time is no evidence of absence from a forbidden region and the scheme is not tamper-proof, so the headline's false-accept rate against added delay, relays or spoofing is not reported. Timed co-location challenges across N chips: no work. Robustness of on-chip GPS to commercial spoofers is a related sub-question, not in the headline, with no work.
doc: Alpay & Alpay (2026), Unprivileged Topology Certificates for Cloud GPU Attestation, arXiv 2606.24934
quote: 169 RIPE Atlas probes place the B200 within 44 km of its claimed datacentre and reject all 11 decoy sites.

scope: Amodo's own report of its own work, not independently checked: a central controller leases bandwidth and transfer-volume quotas to BlueField DPUs over an encrypted tunnel, the DPUs enforce them in software with the Linux traffic controller, and the system runs on one research server; hardware acceleration on BlueField-2/3 is listed as in progress. Not shown: a hardware-fixed set of permitted peers, attestation of cluster size against a bridging device or reconfiguration, holding a cap at line rate (the RFD lists 'can software tc keep up?' as open), and any training slowdown. Fixing which devices may link and attesting cluster size: paper designs only (RAND 2024 proposes restricting interconnect to a handful of preauthorized chips and says the mechanism 'does not yet exist'; flexHEG proposes verifying cluster configuration and outgoing bandwidth). Training slowdown when traffic is forced off NVLink: no work (RAND's 'might not present a significant performance penalty' is speculation).
doc: AI Security Forum, Requests for Discussion, RFD 029 'NIC-Based Bandwidth Limiting & Interconnect Verification' (Amodo), Implementation Status
doc_date: 2025 (repository commit 2025-12-09; the RFD's frontmatter date 2024-11-27 is a placeholder); accessed 2026-10-15
quote: "Phase 1: Software implementation (complete)" … "DPUs enforce quotas via Linux traffic controller (tc)" … "Running on Amodo research server"

scope: Desk analysis of two designs for copper (NVLink-class) links, a modified switch ASIC that copies sampled traffic from its digital fabric and a bump-in-wire retimer exposing its equalized bitstream, with the author's expectations of about 60 ns added per hop, dependence on the switch or retimer vendor, and at least a year of lead time; nothing built or measured. Milton & Reynolds (Amodo, 2026) likewise describe an optical-electrical-optical retimer tap and an electrical interposer at the transceiver port as designs 'not commercially available' that need to be designed and tested. Full line rate and the trustworthiness of an active device: argued (active electronics add attack surface), not tested. Bidirectional circulator-optics TPU pod links: no work. Peigne-Lefebvre et al. (2026) state NVLink traffic has no physical witness.
doc: Cankaya (2026), Research Note: The Fundamentals and Feasibility of Secure Network Taps for Verifying AI Datacenter Use (Substack), section 3.4 Copper vs. optical
quote: Bump-in-wire retimer tap: Insert a signal retimer into the copper link and extract a digital copy from its internal equalized bitstream.

scope: Desk link-budget analysis for the live leg: baseline optical margins against tap insertion loss, with feasibility thresholds of 1.5 dB and 0.5 dB, for 400G-class multimode links inside a scalable unit and single-mode links between units; the monitor-leg recovery at 53-112 GBaud is left as the harder problem and the author says amplification is probably indispensable at 112 GBaud. No tap built or measured at this problem's lane rates. Milton & Reynolds (Amodo, 2026) reach a similar desk result ('even a 1 dB loss may be unacceptable') and say they plan testing; commercial passive taps exist for 26 GBaud lanes (400G-DR8), below this problem's lane rates, which are the headline's stated difficulty, so that is a cross-reference and not evidence; vendors' statements that 53 GBaud should work are unverified hearsay. Cankaya's fleet-margin argument cites Meta production telemetry (John et al., DTS 2025), not held.
doc: Cankaya (2026), Research Note: The Fundamentals and Feasibility of Secure Network Taps for Verifying AI Datacenter Use (Substack), appendix B.5 link-budget feasibility
quote: Intra-SU multi-mode: Passive taps feasible only at 95/5 with direct cabling. Infeasible with standard structured cabling.

scope: Desk analysis of tap placement (north-south edge, storage fabric, east-west levels) and what each level misses; names copper scale-up racks (NVL72, NVL576) and TPU pods above 9,000 chips as blind spots where a frontier run could complete without crossing a tap; the covert-bandwidth figures are Fermi estimates the author calls informed guesses; no fraction-of-compute figure and no measurement; the author lists a rigorous threat model of covert workloads under each placement as his most important open question.
doc: Cankaya (2026), Research Note: The Fundamentals and Feasibility of Secure Network Taps for Verifying AI Datacenter Use (Substack), section 3.5.2
quote: For most deployments, we expect spine-to-leaf to be the lowest practical level for tapping intra-SU/pod compute fabric.

scope: The authors' own CPU/DPDK benchmark at 400 Gb/s: line-rate hashing for frames of 1500 B and above; at 64 B minimum frames no algorithm reaches line rate within the physical core count; hashing only, with no timestamping or signing, zero loss on real datacenter traffic not shown, and no trusted or simple hardware; not 800G or 1.6T (limited hardware availability); the authors say an FPGA or ASIC is likely needed. Peigne-Lefebvre et al. (2026) still pose formally verified FPGA hashing at 400+ Gbps as open.
doc: Reynolds & Foster (2026), Network Traffic Hashing (Amodo Design note), DPDK Summary
quote: For realistic traffic profiles at 1500B and above, AES-128-GMAC and SipHash-1-3-128 are both capable of sustaining line-rate hashing

scope: A protocol design: tap logic kept minimal and physically inspectable, with the prover tapping the tap's own egress so that processors trusted by one side only can suffice ('watching the watchers'; the note points to a separate design built from commodity hardware with redundant processors). The same note says single-party active wardens 'have been built and tested' in prior work (not held, not named) and that extending them to mutual distrust is non-trivial. Nothing built; no line rate shown; formal verification of tap logic, TLS termination in software-free logic, and a secure alarm channel between distrusting processors are left open; Cankaya's System Overview v0.2 says an FPGA active warden has not been made yet.
doc: Cankaya (2026), Research Note: The Fundamentals and Feasibility of Secure Network Taps for Verifying AI Datacenter Use (Substack), summary (Security risks from the taps)
quote: passive optical splitters on tap egress links can let the Prover observe every bit sent to the Verifier, enabling independent re-computation to confirm taps behave as specified.

scope: The author's own early simulations of network-traffic reproducibility, reported and not published, excluding ML non-determinism; no hash-boundary or payload definition has been specified (the note calls an implementable protocol 'a natural next step'); Amodo's SITREP tags network reproducibility 'Not started' and Reynolds & Foster call the payload definition the most important open question.

scope: A protocol design with a security argument: an auditor-owned passive tap hashes inter-node collective payloads into a Merkle tree that is checked against the declared training at challenge time; the authors list the canonical wire-to-tensor mapping ('not a stable public interface today'), auditing that mapping without trusting the trainer's host, and the absence of any NVLink witness as open problems; the paper's prototype concerns the proof system, not the tap or the attribution. Cankaya (2026) separately proposes per-transfer metadata headers (job ID, tensor type, layer, step) so captured samples can be matched to declared workloads, with negligible overhead asserted, not measured. Detecting an undeclared workload embedded in a declared one at stated error rates: no measurement on real traffic; Baker et al. (2025) call the analysis an unsolved problem.

scope: Desk estimates of the quantities asked: sampling 0.01% of a scalable unit's 256 400G scale-out links through a 1x256 optical circuit switch to one FPGA, about $25,000 per unit or about 0.2% of an inferred $12M unit price; storage-fabric capture sized from bursty traffic (about 40 GB/s peak, 3 GB/s average); Amodo's SITREP gives a worst case of one recomputation NIC per inference front-end NIC and tags sampling taps 'Not started'; the author reports that typical north-south edge traffic composition was unavailable to him. Nothing built or measured; this survey's cost goal of 1% of facility cost is met only on paper.

scope: Desk analysis of key disclosure for tapped encrypted traffic: where encryption runs outside a trusted execution environment the prover can retain session keys and share them after sessions expire; for TEE-encrypted fabrics post-hoc decryption is called fundamentally difficult and an active man-in-the-middle tap is sketched as a possible workaround with unestimated overhead; the security trade-off is argued (taps as a substitute for TEE isolation against a malicious operator), not tested. Throughput cost of any such tap: no work. Security Level 5 encrypted-traffic cruxes were found at a workshop and not resolved.

scope: Honest operator; facility power modelled, not metered (the NLR dataset combines measured workload profiles with facility power from a bottom-up model of the power-delivery components); 2-16 Kestrel nodes of four H100s each running Llama-2 70B LoRA and Stable Diffusion: a node-count report from mean facility power tolerates about plus or minus 15% uniform calibration error. Adversarial workload choice, the headline's condition, is not modelled at facility or distribution level. Cross-references, not evidence, because the headline names facility scale: Kimpson, Baker & Graham's adversarial power bound is for a single A100 and the paper says it offers no facility-level, multi-device version; Rahman & Tajdari measured wall versus NVML power on one workstation under evasion strategies.
doc: Abdelghafar & Kulp (2026), Privacy-Preserving AI Verification via Minimal Information Disclosure, arXiv 2608.02774
quote: When every power value is multiplied by the same calibration factor, the fixed quantizer remains perfect from −15.5% to +18.5% error; failures begin at −16% and +19%. This sweep measures tolerance to uniform calibration error.

scope: Measured on one NVIDIA A100 (energy read from the on-die counter, not a feed meter): a power trace alone cannot rule out between 0.41 and 1.16 machines of undeclared compute per declared machine, against an adversary who chooses numeric format, operand values and idle state; same-SKU transfer checked on three more A100s. One device only, so the facility-level, mixed-fleet and run-size clauses of the headline have no measured bound; time-resolved signals (training-step periodicity) are out of the paper's scope. Lower stages: Baker et al.'s PDU metering and three compute-accounting options (RAND 2025, App. A.6) are a design only; the synchronous-swing and shutdown-verification clauses are stated judgements with no work. A companion simulation study by the same group (October 2026) tracks the training-step rhythm in facility power instead of total energy; it detects synchronous training far more reliably but does not say how much compute is running.
doc: Kimpson, Baker & Graham (2026), Can Power Draw Constrain Covert Compute? Limits of Analogue Verification for AI Governance (arXiv 2610.07476)
quote: "Measurements on NVIDIA A100 GPUs constrain β = 1.16 in the worst case, while adversarial matched-energy strategies are shown to hide at least β = 0.41 of compute."

scope: A desk reference-class analysis of utility electricity records by facility size, using Pilz & Heim's data-centre counts and EIA survey counts: a 10 MW continuous load is visible at the utility level but blends with crypto-mining, continuous-process industrial and campus loads; at 1 MW and 100 kW the paper places the load among flat-load commercial customers "of which the United States has millions", a figure it takes from a count of commercial buildings by floor area (EIA CBECS 2018, Table B6), not by electric load or load factor. No detector built, no interval data analysed and no false-alarm rate, so this survey's false-alarm goal of 0.01 per facility-year is not addressed; assumes utility cooperation; off-grid generation defeats it.
doc: Koopmanschap & Barten (2026), How to Catch a GPU: A Taxonomy of Verification and Enforcement Mechanisms for International AI Agreements (arXiv 2607.22619v1), App. B, Power consumption monitoring

There is no externally distinguishing power signature at this scale."

scope: Measured: a production training trace on DGX-H100 racks shows a large power swing recurring about once a second or slower. Built: GPU power smoothing in NVIDIA GB200 (ramp limits and a power floor), tested on hardware with a synthetic benchmark and simulated on the production trace (10.5% extra energy at a floor of 90% of rated power); rack batteries are modelled. These features exist for grid safety, and they also remove the rhythm a meter would look for; no detector has been tested against them. Dong et al. (2013) show that any meter-based classifier falls to chance once the hidden load's average trace matches the cover load's. A simulation study (Kimpson, Baker & Graham, October 2026) tracks the training rhythm through eight concealment strategies, but battery smoothing defeats it unless a second meter sits between the battery and the chips. The measured results so far point against meter-level detection; nothing shows every method fails.

quote: This paper proposes a multi-faceted approach to mitigate these risks, grounded in real-world production telemetry.

scope: A desk analysis of the visual signature by facility size: cooling-tower arrays (economic above 5–10 MW) on a 2,000 m² footprint are anomalous against EIA building statistics; at 1 MW air-cooled chillers and at 100 kW a container look like ordinary commercial buildings. 'Find undeclared sites' clause only, with no false-positive rate and no search without prior candidates; the 'estimate power use within what error' clause has no held work; thermal, radar and seismic clauses are treated qualitatively (seismic sensing 'a confirmation tool, not a search tool'; vibration dampening could defeat it). The classifier result the authors cite (Clymer 2025: all facilities above 10 MW found, all four below missed) is not held and is not evidence here.

scope: A literature-based estimate assuming the facility is not deliberately hidden; the same source says that with active concealment facilities of 10,000 to 100,000 H100-equivalents cannot be ruled out, that the 10,000 figure rests on a single open analysis and 'does not establish a lower bound on the smallest detectable facility', and that the real bound depends on what intelligence agencies achieve. No detection probability is stated, so this survey's detection goal of 90% is not shown. Supply-chain clause: a desk bound of 'on the order of a million chips unaccounted for' from Epoch's chip tracing. Nothing built or tested; the underlying classifier (Clymer 2025) is not held.

scope: A desk analysis (order-of-magnitude physics and logistics) of thermal, acoustic, optical and SAR detection of a 150 to 200 MW, 100,000-H100-equivalent underwater build, finding construction and maintenance the detectable phases; attribution against offshore wind, platforms and ships' generators is unsolved ('detection is not the same as attribution'); no field measurement, no sensor trial.

quote: Thermal detection of an operational pod is unlikely outside shallow, calm water; acoustic detection is marginally more effective, but faces limitations in attribution; and optical/SAR monitoring is most powerful during construction and maintenance

scope: A proposed procedure only: mutual declaration of existing, in-transit and in-production compute, a supply-chain records audit with inspectors counting final chips, comparison against each side's intelligence, then extension to third nations; no confidence level, no pilot, and the plan itself says unknown compute cannot be brought under verification. Facilities clause: Koopmanschap & Barten's desk analysis finds that with active concealment facilities of 10,000 to 100,000 H100-equivalents cannot be ruled out. Stockpile and secret-production clauses: their rough bound of about a million untraced chips. Exit routes and smuggling: stated limits only (Harack et al., Aarne & Petrie).

Ansari notes metadata collection stops at individual providers (no cross-provider or on-premises coverage); Leklem & Maheshwari propose a monitoring network fed by cloud API patterns and export data; Scher's 'might also use financial intelligence' is a one-line suggestion. Payment-record and financial-intelligence methods have no analysis.

scope: A desk estimate from published production and ownership-tracing figures: roughly a million chips untraced, so an approximate upper bound on the largest hidden cluster; the authors call the exact lower bound hard to estimate from public information. No regime stock audit has been run. The detectable-run clause has only models: Shavit's chip-sampling analysis (unmonitored compute sets an implicit lower bound on detectable run size), Dean's AI 2040 model estimate of about 0.5% of world compute divertible, and the same paper's 10 MW (about 10,000 H100-equivalent) satellite threshold, all paper-only. This survey's run size of 10^24 FLOP is not addressed.

Much of the remaining 4.5 million can likely also be traced, leaving on the order of a million chips unaccounted for. This yields an approximate bound on the size of the largest hidden cluster."

scope: A written analysis of the seed-control channel and the design requirement that closes it (a trusted cryptographic RNG bound to the request, not choosable or biasable by the adversary); no bit count is measured and no seed-controlling adversary is tested. Rinberg et al.'s measured exfiltration bounds (Llama and Qwen) assume trusted randomness, so they do not bear on this headline. Amodo's Stage 1 prototype records that its seed is set by the prover and should be verifier-defined, a documented gap. Speculative decoding and non-Gumbel samplers are unevaluated (DiFR).
doc: Rinberg et al. (2025), Verifying LLM Inference to Detect Model Weight Exfiltration (arXiv 2511.02620v3), Appendix E.5
quote: "If the adversary can manipulate randomness, they can transmit information by selecting seeds/samples while leaving per-step likelihoods within normal ranges. In this regime the verifier’s guarantees degrade sharply: many exfiltration strategies become indistinguishable from benign stochasticity, and a malicious provider could even watermark or backdoor outputs via RNG tampering while remaining white-box undetectable [GKVZ24, CG24]."

scope: For this TEE-based block-commitment scheme, sampling a fraction of layer blocks gives detection probability about 1 − (1 − π)^k against an adversary touching k blocks, implemented in CUDA pipelines and evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B across attack types and block configurations; a source's own system. The slow-recomputation trade-off is only analytic: Amodo's example scheme derives a per-step recompute probability of about 1/k when recomputation takes k steps (p ≈ 0.001 for k = 1000) and notes better strategies may exist. No regime-level audit rate against this survey's detection goal of 90%.
doc: Jin et al. (2026), Trusting What You Cannot See: Auditable Fine-Tuning and Inference for Proprietary AI (arXiv 2603.07466v2), section 5.7
quote: "Even modest verification efforts achieve substantial detection rates. For instance, if an adversary compromises 10% of blocks (k = 100) out of N = 1000 and the client samples only π = 1% of blocks, the detection probability reaches Pdetect ≈ 65%."

scope: A game-theoretic model of a cloud provider detecting threshold evasion, with no empirical data: it locates a detection gap at a fixed FLOP band under FLOP-only reporting and says more models will fill it as software improves; it derives no inspection rate, no gain-to-sanction ratio and no treaty-regime equilibrium. Shavit (2023) section 3.2 gives a closed-form samples-per-year model (a sampling model, not a game). The inspection-game literature held in the collection (Avenhaus and co-authors) models nuclear safeguards, not this regime. The 'thresholds fall over time' clause has no model.
doc: Moon, Vedula, Geneson & Bar-on (2025), Strategies and Detection Gaps in a Game-Theoretic Model of Compute Governance (RAND RRA3686-1), Conclusion
quote: "We analyzed a simple model of evasion and showed that a detection gap exists in the model and contains AI trained on biological sequence data."

scope: Design options only: jointly created firmware reference measurements, and listed ways to attest that verification firmware stays present (secure boot made impossible to disable, a secure counter, randomly timed low-latency attestation); Shavit 2023 proposes signed-firmware enforcement, anti-rollback and early remote attestation of updates. Nothing built or tested. Bypass clause at a lower stage: no held document reports a secure-boot bypass of a data-centre GPU; flexHEG Part 2 describes voltage-glitch attacks on secure boot in general from a source not held; Skorobogatov & Woods 2012 broke an FPGA's protections, not an accelerator's. H100 secure boot and anti-rollback features are reported second-hand (Petrie 2024; Scher & Thiergart) from NVIDIA documents not held.
doc: Baker, Kulp, Marks, Brundage & Heim (2025), Verifying International Agreements on AI: Six Layers of Verification (RAND WR-A4077-1)
quote: To obtain reliable reference measurements when the hardware designer’s measurements are untrusted, without gaining access to private information such as the Prover’s code, one option may be for the Verifier and Prover to jointly create reference measurements by emulating a compliant bootup on a confidentiality-preserving technology (e.g., Confidential Computing).

scope: Design discussion only (flexHEG Part III Appendix A; Part II 'Guarantee Update Process'): forced updates through limited lifetimes or licences that carry a minimum version number; approver-based or k-of-n signing of updates; approver signing keys held in a guarantee processor that serial-numbers what it signs, to prevent secret double-signing of lifetime extensions ('a topic for further research'). Nothing built or independently reviewed. Rollback protection is assumed, not shown. The clause 'constrained so no single party can change the rules' is at a lower stage: the same authors say rules about future rules are 'difficult to articulate', a baseline ruleset would be 'technically very challenging', and there is 'no clear mechanism' to ensure neutral rules.
doc: Aarne & Petrie (2025), International Security Applications of Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part III, ARIA)
quote: Required updates would be implemented by having each update have a limited lifetime, tracked by an onboard clock. … If no new update has been installed before the lifetime runs out, the device locks down.

scope: One independent test of NVIDIA GPU confidential computing under physical attack, and it found a break. Academic researchers built a DDR5 memory-bus probe for under $1,000, extracted Intel's attestation key from a fully trusted Xeon in about 15 minutes, and ran a workload on an RTX 3060 outside any secure enclave while passing H100 confidential-computing attestation relayed from a rented H100, because the GPU attestation is not tied to a specific VM. The break goes through the CPU; the H100's own memory and enclave were not attacked, and both vendors call physical attacks out of scope. An independent reverse-engineering of H100 confidential computing (Gu et al. 2025) finds the boot chain and attestation sound within NVIDIA's threat model, but host-visible plaintext command metadata that allows partial reordering or dropping of firmware calls, unprotected command queues, a transfer-size timing channel and still-readable registers: leaks and partial integrity loss, not a break. No physical attack on a data-centre GPU's HBM is held. A Rowhammer attack on workstation GPUs (Lin et al. 2026, GPUBreach) is a cross-reference: its authors list confidential-computing mode as untested.
doc: Chuang et al. (2026), TEE.fail: Breaking Trusted Execution Environments via DDR5 Memory Bus Interposition (IEEE S&P '26)
quote: proves the CPU interfaces directly with a genuine CC GPU. However, the attestation does not identify what the GPU is running.

scope: Measured on one Huawei Ascend 910A accelerator, a vendor research prototype of firmware-only confidential computing: 0.028-0.91% added inference latency. Single device and inference only; no multi-device or training overhead has been published. A workshop participant reports an unpublished characterisation of training overhead from 2 to 1,024 GPUs; it is not counted, since no numbers are public. Availability: in January 2026 only the H100 offered working confidential computing; cluster-scale confidential computing on Blackwell at near-unencrypted speed is a vendor claim. Link encryption: roughly 3% of compute to encrypt NVLink traffic is a desk estimate.
