quote: introduces minimal performance loss during the inference pass(0.91% in GPT2-neo125M and 0.028% in Llama3-Chat-QA-1.5-8B model

scope: Design only: random-time, firmware-raised HBM snapshots hashed on chip and kept in firmware-only non-volatile memory or signed to a verifier-trusted server; overhead and storage cost discussed qualitatively (synchronised chips hang during a snapshot; terabyte-scale checkpoints). Assumes hardware-security-module features that Harack et al. call 'speculative' and 'not yet available'. Harack Appendix L.4 adds a design sketch for a timed weight-residency challenge of about 50 ms, 'an area for future work'. Nothing built. Related built work: Monfared et al. 2026 measured a gap above 350 ms between HBM-resident and host-RAM-resident 60 GB challenges on an H100, a residency probe rather than an attested snapshot, so a cross-reference.
doc: Shavit (2023), What Does It Take to Catch a Chinchilla? Verifying Rules on Large-Scale Neural Network Training via Compute Monitoring (arXiv 2303.11341v2)
quote: A chip’s weight-shards can be captured by snapshotting the chip’s high-bandwidth memory, which contains the weights. These snapshots must be saved at random times, as otherwise the Prover can swap out the true weights for a fake set of weights right before the scheduled logging.

scope: Proof-of-secure-erasure experiments on H200 hardware, the authors' own report: RAM and HBM wipe estimated at tens of minutes for a GB200 tray; disk wipe about 24 hours for 15 TB, extrapolated from a measured 1 TB NVMe write; challenge-phase time not yet computed; non-wipeable memory targeted below 1 GiB but not yet quantified; network-switch memory listed as open. Challenge clause: Monfared et al. 2026 measured a gap above 350 ms between HBM-resident and host-RAM-resident 60 GB challenges on an H100, with no false-alarm rates; Reuter 2026's roughly 2x margin against host-DRAM caching is an analysis; Bursuc et al. 2024 give provably secure proofs of erasure with round-trip-time bounds (theory). Cankaya's v0.2 draft (dated) says a network-level timing probe telling one node's DRAM from another's 'has not yet been demonstrated'. Both clauses sit in one memory-verification community; not every clause answered.
doc: Reynolds & Jacobi (2026), Memory Wipes - Performance Analysis (Amodo Design Notes)
quote: Writing a full 1 TB gave a final average write speed of 160 MiB/s — much lower than the advertised rate — taking ~1h 35 minutes.

scope: Design only, from a self-deprecated working draft (June 2026, since rewritten; treat as dated): a verifier-side auditing environment built from three independently sourced trusted computing bases whose outputs are compared before leaving an air-gap, plus an instructor-executor split with formally verified logic for the simple parts. Nothing built; no estimate of added attack surface. Recomputation-server hardening has no work (AI 2040: 'needs significant research'; Amodo: 'has not been explored'). Comer et al. 2026 (RAND) design a secure inference facility against nation-state attackers, but prover-side, so a cross-reference.
doc: Cankaya (2026), A System Overview for Near-Term, Low-Trust AI Compute Verification, version 0.2 working draft (LessWrong, archived revision 1.4.0)
quote: At least three distinct TCBs (different supply chains, hardware and software. One trusted by the prover, the verifier and a third-party) make up three small clusters, all inside the prover’s datacenter and inside their own air-gap.

scope: Design and a stated soundness condition only, from a self-deprecated working draft (June 2026; treat as dated): a mutually secure auditing environment from three unilaterally trusted, independently sourced trusted computing bases; the February 2026 workshop report says the approach is 'designed to work with great power adversaries without trusting either side's chips', with specifics 'TBA'. Nothing built. The 'proved sound' clause has no work: AI 2040 calls proving the combination sound 'the open problem'. Hausenloy & Li's 'never trustless, only low-trust' is a position.
doc: Cankaya (2026), A System Overview for Near-Term, Low-Trust AI Compute Verification, version 0.2 working draft (LessWrong, archived revision 1.4.0)
quote: The security of redundant cross-checking hinges on the different devices not having the same vulnerabilities, which means they need to be built from independently sourced components, and not share (too much) code or architectural similarity in general.

scope: Designs only. Petrie (2025) designs an off-switch built from thousands of redundant security blocks per chip and evaluates attack vectors on paper; Petrie's firmware offline licensing (2024) is an earlier design. No on-chip governance mechanism has been fabricated and tested against physical attack. The flexHEG authors mention a power-measurement prototype in one sentence, with no results published; a tamper-responsive enclosure prototype tested against probes is cited in flexHEG Part 2, but its own report has not been located.
doc: Petrie (2025), Embedded Off-Switches for AI Compute, arXiv 2509.07637
quote: This massively redundant architecture is designed to prevent unauthorized chip use, even against sophisticated physical attacks.

scope: A modelled estimate: 3.7-7.9 years for chips with built-in flexHEG hardware to displace older accelerators in frontier AI development, counted from when the manufacturer starts work. Other published estimates: 'at least a few years' (Harack et al. 2025); months for firmware-only mechanisms and 18 months to 4 years for silicon changes (Aarne, Fist & Withers 2024). No estimate has been checked against an actual deployment.
doc: Petrie & Aarne (2025), Technical Options for Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 2)
quote: this estimate predicts 3.7 - 7.9 years for flexHEG with integrated hardware to displace non-flexHEG accelerators in frontier AI development

scope: A design, not a build: the flexHEG Guarantee Processor plus Interlock sitting on the accelerator data path, with four candidate placements and a qualitative latency/throughput trade-off (requirements rise the closer the interlock is to the die). Overhead clause: not analysed anywhere; Ansari 2026 says the performance cost of mediating all chip I/O is 'not yet addressed in the published literature'. Binding clause: only qualitative statements (retrofitted hardware 'may be easier for an attacker to decouple'; flexHEG Part 3 poses how the 'brain' could be integrated so it cannot be easily swapped out as an open question); no pairing scheme, no detection rate. The flexHEG team's power-measurement prototype is a retrofit guarantee processor that makes external measurements and does not sit on the I/O path, so it is a cross-reference, not evidence for this headline.
doc: Petrie & Aarne (2025), Technical Options for Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 2)
quote: The Interlock could be implemented in several ways, including 1) as an IP block within the accelerator die, 2) as a chiplet sitting near the accelerator die, 3) as a part of high bandwidth memory (HBM), or 4) as a separate component that operates as a network relay or switch.

scope: Designs only, nothing built: Petrie's on-die design of about 10,000 redundant licence-checking security blocks with an attack-and-countermeasure table (logic flaws, licence reuse, glitching, focused-ion-beam edits, key extraction); RAND's offline licensing with metered compute budgets (Kulp et al. 2024); CNAS's timed licences as the only robust remote disable (Aarne, Fist & Withers 2024). No shipping accelerator enforces a signed time-limited licence (Harack et al. 2025: 'not yet available'). Downgrade and bypass resistance: asserted, not tested; no red-team of licensing firmware on an AI GPU. Stockpiling: discussed as a risk (cycle-counter banking, powered-off reserve chips) with design responses, nothing shown. Related but not counted as a tested failure of this family: CNAS reports that Nvidia's driver-level hash-rate limiter on consumer GPUs was fully circumvented about a year after release, a different mechanism family reported second-hand.
doc: Petrie (2025), Embedded Off-Switches for AI Compute, arXiv 2509.07637
quote: In this paper, we propose a significantly more secure design that would embed thousands of hardware security blocks into upcoming generations of AI chips. Each security block would individually check for up-to-date usage authorization, and block essential chip operations if this approval is not received.

scope: A protocol sketch with pseudocode: k-of-n multilateral signing of licence and guarantee updates, graded quorums by update type, and signer-set changes by update. No prototype (Ansari 2026: 'No prototype exists'), and the open parts are stated by the proposers themselves: who the licence authority is, how the signer set is bootstrapped, what k and n should be, timeout handling for unresponsive signatories, proofs of non-issuance ('would probably require hardware-backed evidence from all devices that contain the private key'), and the blast radius of a stolen signing key. Abuse resistance of emergency disable: Baker et al. 2025 judge it not to need significant R&D because proposals exist; that is a readiness opinion, not evidence.
doc: Petrie & Aarne (2025), Technical Options for Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 2)
quote: The update process could require that the update (or lack of update) be multilaterally approved by k of n parties, so that no single actor could unilaterally impose excessive restrictions (as discussed for an international context in Part III). The pseudocode in algorithm 1 shows how multi-party update approval could be implemented.

scope: Designs only: RAND's licence-metered throttle (bounded training by operation budget, with a hardware cutoff sketch) and CNAS's on-chip restriction to approved code or models; Scher & Thiergart list inference-only chips and an operation disallow-list as building blocks and call them possibly 'extremely difficult or effectively impossible'. No prototype has refused a non-compliant job in a test (Harack et al. 2025). The circumvention clause has no work: no measured throughput penalty for the best attack, and RAND itself notes a clock-slowing throttle 'might be easy to circumvent with a cheap FIB edit'. Stated limit, not a failure: software-only mechanisms can verify use but not enforce it (Petrie & Aarne 2025).
doc: Kulp et al. (2024), Hardware-Enabled Governance Mechanisms (RAND WR-A3056-1)
quote: When the counter for a functional unit (such as a floating-point multiplier block) exceeds the threshold set by the license, a multiplexer placed before the output of the functional unit can select an alternative output value of zero, ignoring the actual computation results.

scope: Design only: a meter built on existing performance counters with licence-set caps, plus proposed protections (monotonic counters, lockstep redundancy, shielding against fault injection, sanity checks between counters). Nothing fabricated or measured; Ansari 2026 records 'the absence of functional prototypes', and current counters are 'accessible via firmware interfaces and were designed for debugging rather than tamper-resistant governance'. Trusted-time clause: design-level only; CNAS proposes counting clock cycles instead of time because tamper-proof time 'generally is considered very difficult', and RAND says there is 'no airtight defense' against clock attacks. Fault-injection resistance and sanity-check false-alarm rates: no work.
doc: Kulp et al. (2024), Hardware-Enabled Governance Mechanisms (RAND WR-A3056-1)
quote: Since these values are already collected in hardware, additional logic could be added to set a maximum value for each counter, determined by a license.

scope: Idea stage only: a proposed red-team/blue-team exercise to test whether cross-device log analysis catches fabricated logs, not yet run; no design for detecting fabrication.

Four verifier-issued timing probes implemented and run on NVIDIA T4 and H100 GPUs on cloud VMs: proof-of-work, parallel verifiable delay functions, tensor-core GEMM puzzles and a randomly timed VRAM-residency check whose keyed Argon2id pass resists parallel precomputation; solve times separate idle from contended GPUs and HBM-resident from host-resident data (60 GB challenge, more than 350 ms apart). The authors call the probes heuristic indicators, give no false-alarm or miss rates, test no adaptive evader, allow answering on idle identical GPUs, and do not compare cost with recomputation; precomputed or decoy ML work as such is not the tested attack. Cankaya (2025) reports that in his own experiments timing revealed resource contention from hidden parallel work (reported, not published in detail).
doc: Monfared, Ganji, Holcomb & Tajik (2026), Timing and Memory Telemetry on GPUs for AI Governance (arXiv 2602.09369v2)
quote: the timing gap between the two modes exceeds 350 ms, making them trivial to distinguish.

scope: Design only: compute-graph declaration to a guarantee processor, static or dynamic, with a proposed description language and kernel translator, and a back-of-envelope log rate (about 10 KB/s per accelerator, which the authors say 'does not scale well with cluster size' when stored locally). Nothing run on a multi-node job; completeness and overhead unmeasured; falsified-operation detection posed as research questions, not tested. Related built work that is not this mechanism: ShadowScope (Almusaddar et al. 2025) validates single-GPU kernel execution against golden performance-counter traces with a non-adaptive attacker; the headline names multi-node logging, so that single-GPU result is a cross-reference.
doc: Petrie & Aarne (2025), Technical Options for Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 2)
quote: Alternatively, a description language specifically for flexHEG compute graphs could be developed along with tools to translate accelerator kernels into this language.

scope: Proposals and analysis only: random partial recomputation by the guarantee processor, local LLM-based checks, and the authors' own argument that fully automatic on-device compliance checking 'appears unlikely to be feasible'; Reuter, Marks & Baker (2026) give a formal framing (a policy over an algebraic graph; 'functional exclusion' left open). No recomputation fraction has been derived or measured for any detection probability; no automated checker has been run on camouflaged logs. Stated limits: static graphs cannot express mixture-of-experts routing; the relevance of Rice's theorem is 'unclear'.
doc: Petrie & Aarne (2025), Technical Options for Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 2)
quote: a general-purpose way to verify each atomic computation is to use the guarantee processor to randomly re-compute a portion of each result

scope: Built, not measured: Amodo report a working prototype in which a central controller leases traffic quotas to NVIDIA BlueField network cards that enforce them, and hardware-accelerated encryption between nodes, with keys the controller can revoke. Membership by key is a form of the allowed-pairs list the problem asks about, but no peer allow-list has been built as such, and no line-rate or latency figures are published. The full interlock design is in flexHEG Part 2 (Petrie & Aarne 2025), with the network card as the retrofit location; encrypting all NVLink traffic is estimated at about 3% of H100 compute (a desk estimate).
doc: AI Security Forum (2025), Requests for Discussion, RFD 029 NIC-Based Bandwidth Limiting & Interconnect Verification (Amodo)
quote: Got hardware-accelerated encryption working

scope: Software-only CPU emulation of NVIDIA GPU inference arithmetic (L40, L40S, A100, H100 profiles), dense transformer blocks of Qwen3-4B plus one full forward pass; bit-exact against CUTLASS, and against cuBLAS through a per-SKU dispatch catalogue except nvjet kernels on H100 at short sequences. Not mixture-of-experts, not AMD, TPU or Ascend, not training. Slowdown clause: not measured; the appendix estimates CPU need and says the figures 'likely need to be multiplied by at least 10x' for reduction-tree emulation, so that clause is paper-only. Cross-hardware next-token agreement without emulation is about 85% one GPU generation apart (Hausenloy & Li 2026).
doc: Cankaya (2026), Bit-Exact AI Inference Verification Without Performance Tradeoffs, arXiv 2606.00279v2
quote: The emulator matches CUTLASS bit-exactly at every tested hardware/sequence-length combination.

scope: A proposed method with a desk analysis of its error sources: estimate achievable utilisation for a declared workload and cluster, compare with declared operations, and back it with physical signatures when an operator's efficiency exceeds the estimate. No model has been validated against measured runs, no padding or no-op detector has been built, and the false-alarm rate for honest operators is only flagged as a risk ('honest Provers [may be] unable to account for their estimated compute use'). Attacks named without defences shown: secret backend optimisation, speculative decoding (1.5-3x), Pareto-inefficient menu choices, restructuring to minimise logged operations. Cankaya's system overview proposes a resource-occupation simulation cross-compared with throughput, also paper-only.
doc: Baker, Kulp, Marks, Brundage & Heim (2025), Verifying International Agreements on AI: Six Layers of Verification (RAND WR-A4077-1)
quote: For a given workload type and cluster, optimal MFU could be coarsely approximated as the MFU known to have been achieved on similar workloads and clusters, on which there is private and public data (Epoch AI, 2024b). Optimal MFU could be more precisely estimated with theoretical modeling (Erdil and Schneider-Joseph, 2024; Erdil, 2025). Still, significant error bars may remain.

scope: Proposals only, none run on a real distributed run: power-draw times energy-efficiency accounting of total operations (RAND 2025), workload-modelling of achievable utilisation (same source), spot-check zero-knowledge proofs with running cumulative-FLOP attestations (Peigné-Lefebvre, Nguyen & Wang 2026, 'a design, not a build'), and chip-logged weight snapshots with verifier retraining (Shavit 2023). No stated error for any of them on a real run; Ansari 2026 and Peigné-Lefebvre et al. both say no independent primitive for verifying reported training compute exists. Built but not on this quantity: Abdelghafar & Kulp 2026 classify training versus inference from real single-machine telemetry and say their duration tier 'is not a proxy for statutory training-compute thresholds'; Harack's Lawfare example is a code-inspection demonstration, not compute totals. Confidential-computing certificate rows depend on the chip's own enclave, which the headline excludes, so they are related, not evidence.
doc: Baker, Kulp, Marks, Brundage & Heim (2025), Verifying International Agreements on AI: Six Layers of Verification (RAND WR-A4077-1)
quote: To verify the number of total operations done in given AI data centers in some period (from ta to tb ), one approach could be to measure AI chips’ power draw (P) over time (Watts per second), and then multiply it by the chips’ energy efficiency (OP per Watt)

scope: Built and measured: single-GPU training of small models (ResNet-50, 23M parameters, from scratch; GPT-2, 117M, fine-tune) replayed bit-identically across three NVIDIA consumer and workstation GPUs (A40, Titan XP, RTX 2080 Ti), FP64 with logged rounding decisions, at about 1.2-1.4x trainer and 1.3-1.7x auditor time and 18-20 MB of logs per GPT-2 step. Not multi-GPU or distributed (all-reduce ordering unhandled), not low precision, not frontier scale. Throughput-penalty clause: one measured figure elsewhere, Peigné-Lefebvre et al. 2026 report full determinism on a 7B model on 8 H100s costing 1.6-8.2% per step and cite 23-82% overhead for deterministic FlashAttention backward. Fraction-of-steps clause at frontier scale: no work.
doc: Srivastava, Arora & Boneh (2024), Optimistic Verifiable Training by Controlling Hardware Nondeterminism, arXiv 2403.09603v3 (NeurIPS 2024)
quote: A method for two parties, training the same model on different GPU types, to achieve identical training results by logging and sharing rounding decisions

scope: Closest to Done on the list: two independent groups show same-SKU inference replays bit-exactly once batch composition is controlled; what is missing is one run on a second machine at production batch size. Same SKU, same software stack, no floating-point atomics in the kernels, batch size logged (one integer per forward pass); shown for Qwen2.5-7B prefill across physical cards at batch sizes 1, 2 and 4. Corroborated by an independent group with its own method: He & Thinking Machines Lab (2025) report 1,000 identical temperature-0 Qwen3-235B completions with batch-invariant kernels at about 20% matmul throughput loss, on the same server. Not shown: production batch sizes on a second machine; mixture-of-experts under tensor parallelism across machines; INT-quantised models, where Cankaya saw non-determinism in vLLM. Earlier 'bitwise reproducibility is rarely achievable in practice' (Karvonen et al. 2025) describes default stacks and predates both.
doc: Cankaya (2026), Bit-Exact AI Inference Verification Without Performance Tradeoffs, arXiv 2606.00279v2
quote: The within-SKU zeros (A100-SXM4 ↔ A100-PCIe) rule out physical-card variance: yield-binned chips of the same SKU produce bit-identical outputs.

scope: Token-DiFR re-implemented by a third party and run on a tray of H100s against non-adaptive attacks (substituted models including gpt-oss-120b versus 20b, LoRA append and append-on-trigger on Qwen2.5-7B); the best honest-versus-cheating pass-rate gap was about 25%, the threshold must be set per model, and most misses were outputs under 5 tokens. Adaptive-attacks clause: the DiFR paper (Karvonen et al. 2025) shows Token-DiFR robust to one simple adaptive attack (temperature tuned to match mean cross-entropy, which defeats cross-entropy checks); stronger adaptive attacks untested, and Amodo's own note says its testing 'only covers a fraction of possible attacks'. Models tested are well below frontier size; the smallest deviations on Qwen3-30B-A3B 'remain difficult to separate' in the DiFR paper.
doc: Amodo Design (2026), An Inference Verification Prototype, Stage 1 (design note)
quote: Our results add further evidence that Token DiFR can identify different incorrect-model attacks reliably across a small range of prompts.

scope: The authors' own measurements on Llama-2-13B (Table 6): committing overhead 0.26 ms per token, validation time 81 ms, 10 KB of provider GPU memory per token; a measured per-token latency cost, not serving throughput at production batch sizes or end-to-end latency on a deployed service. Amodo's Stage-1 prototype measures verifier GPU utilisation (about 2% versus about 53% for the prover on one H100 tray, small open-weight models) and lists latency and throughput as future work; Karvonen et al. (DiFR) measure record size (1.5 to 30 bytes per token), which is in the statement, not the headline.
doc: Ong et al. (2025), TOPLOC: A Locality Sensitive Hashing Scheme for Trustless Verifiable Inference (ICML 2025)
quote: Time and memory overhead of generating and validating Llama-2-13B inference using established verifiable inference compared to our method.

scope: Measured on real GPUs for three open-weight models (Llama-3.1 8B, Qwen3-8B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B), with A100-served and H200-verified cross-hardware noise, as of late 2025; the authors report robust detection across these architectures. Speculative decoding is not evaluated (vLLM 0.10.0 lacked it) and only a verification algorithm for one variant is proposed in an appendix; constrained decoding and future architectures are untested. The AI 2040 and Amodo calls for developers to keep recomputation algorithms in lock-step with new architectures are marked not started.
doc: Karvonen et al. (2025), DiFR: Inference Verification Despite Nondeterminism
quote: These models cover a wide range of differences between models such as hidden dimensions, training distributions and broader architectural differences such as being dense or mixture-of-experts.

scope: Design only: the AI 2040 and Amodo plan verifies production inference by tapping the prover's network and recomputing on a verifier-trusted server placed inside the prover's data centre, so closed weights never leave; the SITREP marks recomputation-server security 'Not on track'. Amodo asks labs to re-implement its open-weight demo on their own stacks with frontier models (not done); Karvonen et al. state DiFR cannot verify closed-weight providers (a design limit, not a test); Cankaya says proprietary-model verification would need third-party- or hardware-attested deployment (one sentence).
doc: Amodo Design (2026), AI 2040 Plan A: Verification SITREP
quote: Whilst simpler than developing a whole SL5 cluster, the recomputation server needs to sit within the prover's data centre, possibly under their physical control.

scope: A design sketch of a neutral jointly-trusted replay cluster (no external communication, no persistent storage, one cluster per chip type), with further designs in Harack et al. (2025) section 2.5.3 and the Proofworks mutually-trusted-compute document. Nothing built: no costed design, no two-party red team, no measured leak bound. Harack et al.: the barriers are security issues with no publicly-known robust solutions. The workshop note that one ~100-chip neutral datacenter project exists is unattributed and does not count.
doc: Shavit (2023), What Does It Take to Catch a Chinchilla? Verifying Rules on Large-Scale Neural Network Training via Compute Monitoring, Appendix D
quote: "Instead, the Prover and Verifier can agree on a neutral jointly-trusted cluster, which they will use to execute the verification protocol. The Verifier needs to be able to trust in the integrity of the cluster’s computation. The Prover, conversely, needs to trust that the cluster will not reveal its private data, by verifying that it cannot communicate with the outside world and has no persistent storage."

scope: Heuristic Proof-of-Training-Data defences (certified-randomness seed, local memorization tests) tested on GPT-2-124M and Pythia checkpoints against all attacks then published in the Proof-of-Learning literature, at about 1.3% of training compute for the verifier; language models only, single attacks only, composite and adaptive attacks and online RL untested, and the Verifier sees raw data and weights. No formal soundness bound exists: the earlier Proof-of-Learning family (Jia et al. 2021) was broken by Fang et al. (2023), a tested failure of that mechanism family; Shavit (2023) gives the formal PoTT definition and leaves provably secure methods to future work.
doc: Choi, Shavit & Duvenaud (2023), Tools for Verifying Neural Models' Training Data (Proof-of-Training-Data), sections 1 and 4
quote: "Our methods can be run cheaply, adding as little as 1.3% of the original training run’s compute. … The verification strategies we describe are not provably robust, but are intended as an opening proposal"

scope: Inference only: a built, open-source ZK proof system measured on LLaMa-2-13B and OPT-13B (one A100 plus 12 CPU cores): 803 s to prove a 2048-token inference, proof under 200 kB, verification in seconds; impractical at production request rates, and later systems (ZKTorch, zkGPT) remain at GPT-2 to Llama-2-7B scale with minutes per token. Training: no ZK proof of full-LLM backpropagation in native floating point has been shown (Peigné-Lefebvre et al. 2026); their 36-month, single-digit-percent-overhead estimate is a paper estimate, and zkLLM's authors write that ZK proofs of LLM training may pose insurmountable challenges.
doc: Sun, Li & Zhang (2024), zkLLM: Zero Knowledge Proofs for Large Language Models (ACM CCS 2024), Abstract
quote: "for LLMs boasting 13 billion parameters, our approach enables the generation of a correctness proof for the entire inference process in under 15 minutes."

scope: A proof-of-useful-work protocol for matrix multiplication over a finite field with near-zero prover overhead; security rests on a new hardness conjecture; no implementation, benchmark or attack evaluation. It proves a lower bound on matmul work done, not that a declared workload ran, and says nothing about privacy or about non-AI scientific workloads (weather, CFD, protein folding), which have no work. The Proofworks proof-of-memory protocol (Reuter & Karvonen 2025, preliminary fingerprint experiments) verifies declared AI workloads generally and is a neighbouring compute-accounting problem.
doc: Komargodski & Weinstein (2025), Proofs of Useful Work from Arbitrary Matrix Multiplication (arXiv 2504.09971v4), Abstract
quote: "Our main result is a PoUW for the task of Matrix Multiplication MatMul(A, B) of arbitrary matrices with 1 + o(1) multiplicative overhead compared to naïve MatMul. We conjecture that our protocol has optimal security in the sense that a malicious prover cannot obtain any significant advantage over an honest prover."

scope: One component measured: hashing every frame on one 400GbE link, on a 64-thread server CPU and on a BlueField-3 network card, to build a log for later checking. No commitment protocol or neutral-site verification has been built, and nothing has been demonstrated end to end on a real workload. The design for the full loop is in Harack et al. (2025), which says no existing system does this and that cost, difficulty and time at scale are unanswered.
doc: Reynolds & Foster (2026), Network Traffic Hashing (Amodo design note)
quote: SipHash-1-3-128 clears 400 Gbps at every packet size tested

scope: Leakage measured as estimated conditional mutual information on real physical-measurement datasets (GPU power, telemetry and electromagnetic traces, including H100 and B200 nodes) across six verification tasks, with one release certified by a Groth16 zk-SNARK; a source reporting its own method. Not a provable information-flow bound: estimation is unreliable for high-dimensional traces, protection holds only under the design distribution of the development data, and nothing is tested against repeated queries, data fusion or a state adversary (Daley: filterability against a state adversary is not established).
doc: Abdelghafar & Kulp (2026), Privacy-Preserving AI Verification via Minimal Information Disclosure (arXiv 2608.02774v1), Abstract
quote: "Across these tasks, MID produces three releases with perfect held-out verification and zero measured collateral leakage, while the remaining tasks yield explicit privacy–utility frontiers."

scope: External power draw of a single NVIDIA H200 NVL sampled at 10 MHz, 5 s traces, 17 LLM families and 25 non-AI workloads, authors' own classifier; four evasion strategies tested by the authors, who say this is not a comprehensive adversarial evaluation: three caught at or above 99%, diluted LoRA at 48-88% without the rescue rule, below this survey's detection goal of 90%; cross-device and cross-generation generalisation 'remains to be established'; single node. Corroborating own-method report: Rahman & Tajdari (2026) classify training against non-training from zero-overhead GPU telemetry at 98.2% across 9 GPU types, single node up to 8 GPUs, with dilution and idle-padding evasion tested. Harack et al. (2025) 'not yet possible to reliably know' predates both.
doc: Gargiulo & Kulp (2026), Workload Identification with Physical Side Channels for AI Governance, arXiv 2609.00309, abstract
quote: "we separate training from inference and from non-AI computation with an accuracy of 97% and a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.955, evaluated on model families unseen during training" … "The fourth, diluted low-rank adaptation (LoRA), is detected 48–88% of the time with a hardened classifier"

scope: Hidden inference on parallel CUDA streams alongside re-executed LLM inference on identical hardware, detected by timing with numerical fingerprinting as a complement; the author's own experiments, unquantified (no fraction of declared compute, no detection rate). The second clause, how much compute can be freed undetectably, has only paper-only work: Reuter's expectation for his own proposed protocol (1-2%) and a verifiable-memory-exhaustion draft with placeholder results. Bounding hidden memory and model-swap time: nothing built.
doc: Cankaya (2025), Catching Misreporting About ML Hardware Use by Turning Noise into Signal, Part I (Substack)
quote: Any significant hidden workload would contend for resources, causing detectable slowdowns. In my experiments, resource contention was evident in timing.

scope: A design: a verifier-developed classifier that the deployer must run on all inputs and outputs, with coverage ensured by weight containment plus cluster-level batch authorization; the authors rate feasibility 'Medium; 1-2 years'; nothing built or measured for either clause. Proving coverage to an outside inspector: paper only (also flexHEG Part 1's inference receipts). Catching misuse among approved traffic at a stated false-positive rate: paper only; the authors argue low sensitivity may be tolerable. Compute diverted before telemetry flags it: Hausenloy & Li's second-hand claim is not evidence.
doc: Scher & Thiergart (2024), Mechanisms to Verify International Agreements About AI Development (MIRI; arXiv June 2025)
quote: One major hurdle is ensuring that all relevant inputs and outputs are passed through the classifier. One way to achieve this is to both: prevent weights from leaving the data center, and have close monitoring of all chips in the data center.

scope: A desk analysis of the headline's question: detection must use volume and routing; DiLoCo-style training at under 40 Mbps sits below average household upload speed; jitter, variable-rate streaming, pauses and VPN routing can disguise it, so the author expects the requirements to favour evaders. The 40 Mbps figure comes from the paper's simulation, not a measured run. No classifier designed, trained or tested on traffic; no detection or false-positive rate for this survey's goals. Moon et al.'s large-data-transfer threshold is a proposal for detecting training through cloud ingress, a neighbouring question. Koopmanschap & Barten's note that concealment removes the signature is an argument.
doc: Rahman (2026), Does Distributed Training Undermine Compute Governance? (MIRI; arXiv 2605.29359)
quote: any efforts at detecting distributed training by monitoring internet traffic would have to rely on analysis of the volume and routing, not on the content … the traffic can be disguised into almost any irregular pattern. Traffic shaping methods include jitter, variable-rate streaming, and intermittent pauses.

scope: A built LLM-auditor prototype (TEE and attestation emulated on a CPU without SEV; frontier model called remotely) evaluated on 21 real codebases: perfect discrimination of correct from wrong papers on objective questions, less stable on subjective ones; the audit task is software-artifact verification, not compute verification. The 'when' clause has no timeline estimate. Resistance to jailbreaks, prompt injection and backdoors: not tested; the author concedes prompt injection cannot be prevented and designs for it to leave evidence in a signed transcript.
doc: Rowstron (2026), Agentic Witnessing: Pragmatic and Scalable TEE-Enabled Privacy-Preserving Auditing (ARIA; arXiv 2604.24203)
quote: We demonstrate this architecture by automating the artifact evaluation process for 21 peer-reviewed computer science papers with released codebases on GitHub (e.g. Does the codebase implement the system described in the paper?). We verified five high-level properties of these codebases described in the corresponding publications, treating the source code as private.

scope: Simulated (a distributed-training cost model calibrated to Covenant-72B, not a measured run): adds a 1,280 GB HBM memory threshold beside the 16-H100-equivalent cluster line for a 10^25 FLOP evasion, showing memory capacity, not only FLOP/s, matters for scope. Consumer/edge clause: the same desk analysis places 4-8 GPU workstations, DGX-class servers and GDDR parts below that threshold, also paper only. No throughput-prediction study; nothing measured. '1025' is the saved text's rendering of 10^25.
doc: Rahman (2026), Does Distributed Training Undermine Compute Governance? (MIRI), arXiv 2605.29359
quote: imposing the memory limit reduces the maximum unregistered per-node model from 240B to roughly 91B parameters, forces the evader to operate approximately five times as many nodes for equivalent model quality, and raises the cost of illicitly developing a 1025 FLOP model by roughly 50%.

scope: Evasion clause only: a simulated cost of structuring a 10^24, 10^25 or 10^26 FLOP run as clusters below every proposed registration threshold (DiLoCo-family methods over 100 Mbps links; extrapolated 10-300x beyond tested model size). The same paper proposes a 1,280 GB HBM memory threshold as a fix to the threshold definition, also paper only. Which compute counts (fine-tuning, distillation, mixture-of-experts, inference scaling) and how thresholds are renegotiated: no work beyond framing and stated difficulties.
doc: Rahman (2026), Does Distributed Training Undermine Compute Governance? (MIRI), arXiv 2605.29359
quote: these proposed or existing regulations could be evaded using $1.6M, $31M, and $3.8B, respectively, of hardware arranged in clusters smaller than any proposed registration requirement

scope: Experiments on GPT-2 (124M parameters, OpenWebText) and published Pythia checkpoints: a glued transcript (two training runs reported as one continuous run, i.e. a run resumed from another run's checkpoint) is caught by a weight-norm jump and a memorization cut-off at the join; the verifier holds data, weights, code and checkpoints. The opposite direction (one long run reported as many 'fresh' short runs) rests on the certified-random initialisation design, argued hard to spoof but not tested; no false-link rate at frontier scale; laundering of a checkpoint through declared 'training data' not covered.
doc: Choi, Shavit & Duvenaud (2023), Tools for Verifying Neural Models' Training Data, arXiv 2307.00682
quote: Below, we show that our methods address existing attacks from the literature (Glue-ing and Interpolation), and also demonstrate our method’s response to two new attacks (Data Addition and Subtraction).

scope: Simulated cost for 10^25 FLOP of local-equivalent compute with DiLoCo-family methods over 100 Mbps links and nodes below 16 H100-equivalents; extrapolated 10-300x beyond tested model size and up to 250x in replica count; calibrated against Covenant-72B but not a measured run. No bandwidth at which training becomes uneconomic is identified; the paper's cost table spans 10 Mbps to 1 Gbps.
doc: Rahman (2026), Does Distributed Training Undermine Compute Governance? (MIRI), arXiv 2605.29359
quote: At 100 Mbps bandwidth, it costs about 3× more to do training distributed relative to centralized, but it is not a substantial barrier to feasibility.

scope: Proof-of-Training-Data tested on GPT-2 (124M) and Pythia (70M) checkpoints: catches gluing, interpolation, data subtraction and large data additions for about 1.3% of training compute; the verifier is given data, weights and code. The headline's backdoor clause is not met: the authors concede the method is not robust to small additions of harmful data (quoted by Reuel et al.). Composition rules (e.g. code-token fraction) and privacy-preserving membership proofs have designs only (Scher 2026; flexHEG Part 1); verifying that claimed data origins are uncompromised: no work.
doc: Choi, Shavit & Duvenaud (2023), Tools for Verifying Neural Models' Training Data, arXiv 2307.00682
quote: We show experimentally that our verification procedures can catch a wide variety of attacks, including all known attacks from the Proof-of-Learning literature.

scope: Delegation setting: a client fixes the program and several untrusted providers run it; a referee localises any divergence to one training step and one operator, re-executes it and rules, so an execution that departs from the declared program is caught given bitwise reproducibility (the RepOps library). Implemented and benchmarked on DistilBERT and Llama-3.1 1B and 8B training and inference, FP32 only, about 60% overhead on an A100. Not shown: a prover who both writes and mis-declares the code, frontier scale, or any check of the declaration's content (architecture, optimiser schedule) beyond re-execution; Choi et al. (2023) re-execute segments of a declared transcript on GPT-2 in the same spirit, for data rather than code.
doc: Arun et al. (2025), Verde: Verification via Refereed Delegation for Machine Learning Programs, arXiv 2502.19405
quote: Our implementation shows that refereed delegation achieves both strong guarantees for clients and practical overheads for compute providers.

scope: Served-model identity by recomputation on one 8xH100 server with prover and verifier on the same box; open-weight 7B-120B models; developer-run attacks (model substitution, LoRA append, append-on-trigger); 37,500 prompt runs; a fixed threshold gave honest-prover failures and short-output false negatives. The evaluated-versus-deployed clause (a TEE-signed hash of weights and code) is a design only, which Scher & Thiergart call 'mostly solved in principle'; no real pilot, which the headline asks for; handling of legitimate model versions: no work.
doc: Amodo (2026), An Inference Verification Prototype — Stage 1 (Amodo Design note)
quote: Our results add further evidence that Token DiFR can identify different incorrect-model attacks reliably across a small range of prompts.

scope: A design and estimate from 2023: random sampling of chips' logged weight snapshots, with a formula for the samples needed to catch a rule-breaking run at a given probability. For a 10^25 FLOP run among 10^7 chips, caught within 30 days at 90% probability: about 232,000 samples a year, or about 232 inspectors if each checks 1,000 chips a year (an assumption), against 280 IAEA inspectors in 2021. No cost estimate and nothing run; it assumes chips that log weight snapshots, which still do not exist in 2026, and no later paper has updated the numbers. The installed base has roughly reached his assumption (over 15 million H100-equivalents in January 2026, Epoch AI), and 10^25 FLOP is now an ordinary run rather than a frontier one.
doc: Shavit (2023), What Does It Take to Catch a Chinchilla? Verifying Rules on Large-Scale Neural Network Training via Compute Monitoring
quote: This would require ≈ 232 inspectors, slightly smaller than the 280 active IAEA inspectors as of 2021.

scope: A proposed design (automatic compute-anomaly triggers inside a three-layer inspectorate) that answers the trigger clause on paper; the great-power-patron clause rests on the authors' reading of the historical record, and their analysis of challenge inspections in the Alva Myrdal Centre treaty database is not yet reported; no false-alarm rate and no trigger calibration, which the authors call 'the substantive work ahead'. The Proofworks observation that no challenge inspections have been implemented between great powers and Koopmanschap & Barten's point that power monitoring needs utility cooperation are context and a stated limit.
doc: Leklem & Maheshwari (2026), How Should We 'Inspect' Artificial Intelligence? (Alva Myrdal Centre insights)
quote: formal challenge inspections historically go uninvoked when a violator has a great-power patron, so verification cannot depend on a state being willing to accuse.

scope: Whistleblower clause only: a draft treaty article (Article X) with anti-retaliation duties, confidential or anonymous reporting channels run by the treaty body, identity protection, and asylum for whistleblowers and their families; a proposal, untested. The certainty personnel-based verification can give: no work beyond Harack's stated limit ('achievable certainty might be much lower than ... with hardware'). Survival against staff under video surveillance or with backdoored computers: Baker et al. state the limit, no design. Reach into state-run operations abroad: Rahman states the limit.
doc: Scher, Abecassis, Barnett & Abeyta (2025), An International Agreement to Prevent the Premature Creation of Artificial Superintelligence (MIRI), arXiv 2511.10783 v3
quote: Parties prohibit and prevent retaliation against Covered Whistleblowers and Associated Persons, including but not limited to dismissal, demotion, blacklisting, loss of benefits, harassment, intimidation, threats, civil or criminal actions, visa cancellation, physical violence, imprisonment, restriction of movement, or other adverse measures.

scope: A draft treaty article (Article XI, modelled on Articles IX, XII and XIV of the Chemical Weapons Convention): notification, 36-hour acknowledgement and 5-day clarification, Executive Council adjudication with a challenge inspection, then graded measures (added monitoring, hardware relinquishment, sanctions, protective actions); a proposal, untested. Aggregating graded evidence (many sub-threshold acts) and attributing a violation to the responsible actor (cloud provider versus customer, runs split across providers) have no design; Moon et al.'s call for an agency able to unmask evaders is framing.
doc: Scher, Abecassis, Barnett & Abeyta (2025), An International Agreement to Prevent the Premature Creation of Artificial Superintelligence (MIRI), arXiv 2511.10783 v3
quote: The Concerned Party notifies the Requested Party of their concern, while also sharing their concern with the Director-General and Executive Council. The Requested Party will acknowledge this notification within 36 hours, and provide clarification within 5 days.

scope: Delegation setting: when two executions of the same ML program disagree, a referee bisects by checkpoint hashes to one training step and one operator, re-executes it and rules; benign floating-point mismatches are removed by bitwise-reproducible operators, implemented and benchmarked on DistilBERT and Llama-3.1 1B and 8B in FP32. It finds which party is wrong, not whether the cause was a hardware fault or cheating; no baseline rate of benign replay mismatches is measured; Cankaya (2026) claims his own bitwise replay settles statistical false alarms, a self-report at the same stage; GPU-stack training replay at frontier scale not shown.
doc: Arun et al. (2025), Verde: Verification via Refereed Delegation for Machine Learning Programs, arXiv 2502.19405
quote: we design Verde, a dispute arbitration protocol that efficiently handles the large scale and graph-based computational model of modern ML programs. For (2), we build RepOps (Reproducible Operators), a library that eliminates hardware “nondeterminism” by controlling the order of floating point operations performed on all hardware. Our implementation shows that refereed delegation achieves both strong guarantees for clients and practical overheads for compute providers.

scope: One 8xH100 server with prover and verifier on the same box; open-weight 7B-120B models; inference only; developer-run attacks (model substitution, LoRA append, append-on-trigger); 37,500 prompt runs; completeness ignored; a fixed threshold gave honest-prover failures and short-output false negatives. Not an independent red team, no national-security team, no two-state experiment, no leak or warning-time measurement; Reynolds & Foster's line-rate hashing benchmark is a second self-run component test. Red-team exercises of the stack and a joint international experiment: no work (Baker et al., early 2025: the listed challenges 'mostly receive little to no work').
doc: Amodo (2026), An Inference Verification Prototype — Stage 1 (Amodo Design note)
quote: Our results add further evidence that Token DiFR can identify different incorrect-model attacks reliably across a small range of prompts.

scope: A draft treaty's proposed response ladder (diplomacy, sanctions, escalation to disruption), with the same text separating detection of covert violations from nonproliferation and enforcement; proportionality is specified only for domestic penalties on restricted research (Article IX: 'proportionate to the severity of the violation and ... designed to act as a sufficient deterrent'). Nothing modelled, tested or exercised; no attribution procedure. Baker et al. (RAND 2025, Table 4) list the same options (reciprocation, sanctions, export controls, withdrawal of guarantees, cyber or kinetic attacks, technical mechanisms) and note they 'would ideally be effective deterrents and thus never carried out'; Harack et al. put most enforcement outside their scope.
doc: Scher, Abecassis, Barnett & Abeyta (2025), An International Agreement to Prevent the Premature Creation of Artificial Superintelligence (MIRI; arXiv 2511.10783), overview of the agreement
quote: "Should nonproliferation fail, or if a rogue actor is found to be working towards ASI, coalition members can employ their agreed-upon enforcement mechanisms. These start with standard tools of international pressure such as diplomacy and economic sanctions. Depending on the nature of the developments, countries could escalate to other means at their disposal to disrupt, slow, or impede ASI development."

scope: An empirical result from the Alva Myrdal Centre Arms Control Agreement Database (99 compliance mechanisms, 33 treaties, 1959 to 2015) on one leg only, the inspector model. Powers, decision-making, staffing, trigger calibration, access provisions and registry governance have paper proposals at most (the authors' three-layer inspectorate; Harack et al. and Scher treat body design as political and out of scope), and the authors call them 'the substantive work ahead'.
doc: Leklem & Maheshwari (2026), How Should We 'Inspect' Artificial Intelligence? (Alva Myrdal Centre insights)
quote: The scope of the agreement is strongly associated with the inspector model. Bilateral treaties use party-on-party inspectors 95% of the time; multilateral treaties use institutional inspectors 47.4% of the time, roughly 10× the bilateral rate of 4.9%.

scope: A paper mapping of candidate agreement types (compute caps, mandated evaluations, public reporting, non-proliferation, ruleset-based agreements) onto claims a flexHEG device could check; the same report poses the translation question as open for military cyber-physical systems. Harack et al. (2025) analyse verification requirements by agreement type in their section on agreements. The mapping from machine-checkable artifacts (receipts, audit trails) to legal instruments raised by AI 2040 has no worked example; nothing implemented.
doc: Aarne & Petrie (2025), International Security Applications of Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 3)
quote: Verification of such claims could be used to verify compliance with formal agreements regarding any of the above, such as agreements not to train models above a given size or capability level, agreements to ensure that models always need to attain sufficient scores on particular safety evaluations, or agreements to simply publicly report the results of verifiable evaluations.

scope: One leg only, non-interference with national technical means: a count from the Alva Myrdal Centre treaty database (99 mechanisms, 33 treaties, 1959 to 2015) showing such clauses exist only in bilateral treaties, so a multilateral AI treaty's clause would be novel; Scher (2026) notes SALT I to New START authorise NTM and prohibit interference (precedent). Cross-border retention of captured data (Cankaya: 'will vary on a case-by-case basis') and defensive jamming (Cankaya: 'out-of-scope') have no work. Teague et al.'s estimate that passive acoustic sensors would need to sit inside the 12-nautical-mile territorial sea is for the statement's territorial-waters clause, not the headline (related).
doc: Leklem & Maheshwari (2026), How Should We 'Inspect' Artificial Intelligence? (Alva Myrdal Centre insights)
quote: All 10 NTM non-interference clauses and all 7 concealment prohibitions in the dataset are bilateral.

scope: A plan-level proposal: US–China mutual declaration first (about 85% of global compute), then extension to the 5–10 other compute-hosting nations to reach 99%, with urgency tied to intelligence uncertainty about those nations' compute; no mechanism for securing participation and no modelling of a partial agreement. Baker et al. (RAND 2025, Table 4) list options for attaining participation (export controls and energy policy to keep hardware in cooperative states, dialogues, leverage). Non-participants clause: Harack et al. (2025) note only that protocols for non-global agreements 'may have to take into account the existence of non-participating states'; Daley poses the dependence on other states; host-state seizure (Harack et al.) is a stated risk.
doc: Dean (2026), Verification Plan (AI 2040 Plan A supplement, AI Futures Project), Phase 2, top priority recommendation 1
doc_date: 2026 (no date on page; companion documents dated 2 Jul 2026; read 2026-10-15)
quote: "Extend this declaration to other countries with significant compute ownership or production capacity. Do so urgently unless there is confident intelligence in place that would detect this compute being moved."

scope: A qualitative desk comparison of three routes to a trusted standard (adapting existing commercial designs, open-source projects such as OpenTitan, seL4 and Caliptra, and a de novo international collaboration), weighing the security limits of commercial designs and the precedent of weakened encryption standards; no review conducted, no standard written, no state's position recorded. Standards for assessing other parties' solutions, trust in lab findings and an appliance standard: calls for work only.
doc: Aarne & Petrie (2025), International Security Applications of Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees (flexHEG Part 3), Establishing Trust in Existing Designs
quote: "Concerns about subtle vulnerabilities could likely be addressed through a detailed international review of the design, where each design choice is carefully justified to ensure that it was not animated by any ulterior motive. However, sufficiently suspicious states may still insist that the only acceptable long-term solution is a de novo design."

scope: Funding only, as a proponent's unsourced figures: a $50 to 150M capitalisation recommended for one central project, against 'less than $15M' spent on verification technologies to date (same document, AI-lab section). People and manufacturing capacity are not estimated: the companion SITREP lists 'preparing plans for quick and secure scaled-up manufacturing' as an extension and Proofworks notes a multi-month manufacturing buffer. No survey of the field's funding or headcount.
doc: Amodo Design (2026), AI 2040 Plan A: How You Can Help
quote: Fund a large central project to “own” Plan A verification. Their goal should be to ensure AI verification technology can be deployed in early 2029. The remit would cover not just the R&D but also the stockpiling and planning for scale-out. Before the end of 2026, they should be capitalised with at least $50-150M, and as the project succeeds, they should expect to scale to absorb more funding.

scope: A desk mapping of agreement families (transfer knowledge, transfer resources, pool resources, prepare for emergencies, regulate development and deployment) to verification requirements and to mechanisms judged effective, mature and politically viable, including the conclusion that 'a true ban is likely impossible via blunt mechanisms, but is potentially workable via fine-grained controls'. The 'civilian not military' and 'not building prohibited AI' claims are posed by Harack (2026) without a feasibility result; a speed limit or pause: no work. Evidence-granularity clause: Cankaya asserts collision-resistant per-workload capture as a requirement and asks whether token-level capture is reasonable (self-deprecated v0.2); no work beyond that. Nothing piloted or negotiated.
doc: Harack et al. (2025), Verification for International AI Governance (Oxford AIGI), §4 (possible agreements and their verification requirements)
quote: "This section provides an overview of possible international agreements relating to AI and their verification requirements." … "These were chosen because they appear to be a compelling combination of a) effective, b) technologically mature, and c) politically viable."

scope: A literature-based feasibility taxonomy of about twenty hardware-governance mechanisms by an author outside the proponent groups; by its own limitations section the ratings come from the author's reading 'rather than from formal expert elicitation or independent technology readiness review'; no comparison of independent ratings against proponents' own. The per-family timelines in the sources (Cankaya: off-chip mechanisms in testing and de-risking as of July 2026; Harack et al.: a one-year crash program; Aarne et al.: about four years for on-chip uptake) are proponents' estimates and belong to those families' problems.
doc: Ansari (2026), Hardware-Level Governance of AI Compute: A Feasibility Taxonomy for Regulatory Compliance and Treaty Verification (arXiv 2604.04712v1)
quote: Our analysis reveals a structural mismatch: the mechanisms most needed for treaty verification … are also the least mature.

scope: One mechanism measured in the lab, not a stack in a pilot: making a small Llama model's computation reproducible for dispute checking costs about 60% extra time for training and inference on one A100. Device-cost estimate: monitoring hardware of hundreds to a few thousand dollars per rack against racks costing millions (Cankaya 2026, an order-of-magnitude estimate that leaves out guarding, inspection, recomputation and staff). No full verification stack has been piloted, so a cost of about 1% of a facility's cost is not shown.
